summary: Observation tower on the Gettysburg battlefield, 60 feet tall. The park service dates it to 1896, a 2008 blog to 1895; sources differ on the builder.

facts.design: 60-foot metal observation tower with a roofed platform at the top
facts.agency: National Park Service, Gettysburg National Military Park

access.note: On the Gettysburg battlefield. The park service describes it as a primary place for people to view and study the battlefield.

events.note: The park service credits the Gettysburg Battlefield Commission with completing it in 1896. A 2008 Gettysburg Daily post gives 1895.

evidence.supports: tower stands on the summit of the hill on the Gettysburg battlefield
evidence.quote: Today the summit of the hill is topped with an observation tower and several Union monuments and markers
On July 2nd & 3rd, 1863, it was the target of attacks by the Confederate 2nd Corps.

evidence.supports: held by Union defenders at various times
evidence.quote: At various times it was held by Union defenders from the 12th Corps

evidence.supports: from the top, most of the battlefield can be seen
evidence.quote: From the top of the Culp’s Hill Observation Tower you can view most of the battlefield.

evidence.supports: park service: completed by Gettysburg Battlefield Commission in 1896
evidence.quote: The Gettysburg Battlefield Commission completed the Culp's Hill Observation Tower in 1896.

evidence.supports: Gettysburg Daily gives 1895 and original military study purpose
evidence.quote: The Culp’s Hill Tower was built in 1895. It stands sixty feet above the summit of the hill, and was originally constructed for military study of the battlefield.

evidence.supports: Stone Sentinels: War Department, five towers in the 1890s, three still exist
evidence.quote: The tower is one of five put up in the 1890’s by the War Department, three of which still exist today.

evidence.supports: marker: War Department built the observation tower
evidence.quote: In later years the United States War Department would build avenues and construct the observation tower behind you.
In 1864 the Gettyburg Battlefield Memorial Association purchased land here, some of the first preserved battlefield land in American history.
The Culp’s Hill Observation Tower is a 60-foot tall metal tower with a roofed platform at the top.

evidence.supports: platform reached by seven flights of stairs
evidence.quote: The platform can only be accessed by climbing 7 flights of stairs.

evidence.supports: primary place to view and study the battlefield
evidence.quote: Since that time, is has been a primary location which people can view and study the terrain of the battlefield.

evidence.supports: small parking area loops around the summit
evidence.quote: A small parking area loops around the summit.

corrections.why: The park service page is titled Culp's Hill Observation Tower. The 'Historic' wording comes from the OpenStreetMap record.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The park service says the Gettysburg Battlefield Commission completed the tower in 1896; a 2008 Gettysburg Daily post says 1895. Stone Sentinels and the HMdb marker credit the War Department. The event uses 1896 from the park service.

sources.title: Observation tower on the summit of Culp's Hill on the Gettysburg battlefield

notes_for_editor: Identity and design are consistent across four sources. The build date (1895 or 1896) and builder (Battlefield Commission or War Department) are disputed and the story says so. OSM gives height 18 m; the NPS 60-foot figure is 18.3 m, and the fact uses 18.3. Proposed name correction is for review only. The Stone Sentinels and Gettysburg Daily pages are undated or dated 2008; no current condition or hours source was found.
